title: Server and Hybrid Rendering
description: Learn about server-side rendering (SSR), prerendering (SSG), and hybrid rendering in Angular: server routing (app.routes.server.ts), RenderMode, getPrerenderParams, redirects, authoring server-compatible components, DI tokens (REQUEST, RESPONSE_INIT), HttpTransferCache, and server configurations.

blocks.text: Angular ships all applications as client-side rendered (CSR) by default. While this approach delivers an initial payload that's lightweight, it introduces trade-offs including slower load times, degraded performance metrics, and higher resource demands since the user's device performs most of the computations. As a result, many applications achieve significant performance improvements by integrating server-side rendering (SSR) into a hybrid rendering strategy.
What is hybrid rendering?

Hybrid rendering allows developers to leverage the benefits of server-side rendering (SSR), pre-rendering (also known as "static site generation" or SSG) and client-side rendering (CSR) to optimize your Angular application. It gives you fine-grained control over how the different parts of your app are rendered to give your users the best experience possible.
Setting up hybrid rendering
You can create a new project with hybrid rendering by using the server-side rendering flag (i.e., --ssr) with the Angular CLI ng new command:
You can also enable hybrid rendering by adding server-side rendering to an existing project with the ng add command:

By default, Angular prerenders your entire application and generates a server file. To disable this and create a fully static app, set outputMode: "static" in angular.json. To enable SSR, update the server routes to use RenderMode.Server.
Server routing
You can create a server route config by declaring an array of ServerRoute objects in app.routes.server.ts:

code: path: '', // This renders the "/" route on the client (CSR)
path: 'about', // This page is static, so we prerender it (SSG)
path: 'profile', // This page requires user-specific data, so we use SSR
path: '**', // All other routes will be rendered on the server (SSR)

Rendering modes

rows: Renders the application on the server for each request, sending a fully populated HTML page to the browser.
Renders the application in the browser. This is the default Angular behavior.
Prerenders the application at build time, generating static HTML files for each route.

blocks.text: Choosing a rendering mode

items: Client-side rendering (CSR): Simplest development model running entirely in the browser. Best for authenticated dashboards or offline experiences with Service Workers.

Server-side rendering (SSR): Faster initial page loads and excellent SEO, as crawlers receive fully rendered HTML documents. Code cannot depend strictly on browser APIs, and each request consumes server CPU.
Build-time prerendering (SSG): Fastest possible page loads and CDN caching. All information must be known at build-time with no user-specific data.

Redirects

items: Server-Side Rendering (SSR): Redirects are performed using standard HTTP redirects (e.g., 301, 302) within the server-side rendering process.
Prerendering (SSG): Redirects are implemented as "soft redirects" using <meta http-equiv="refresh"> tags in the prerendered HTML.

Authoring server-compatible components
Browser globals like window, document, and localStorage do not exist on the server. Wrap browser-specific code in afterNextRender or afterEveryRender hooks:

code: import { Component, ElementRef, viewChild, afterNextRender } from '@angular/core';
// Safe: only runs in the browser, not the server

blocks.text: Avoid using isPlatformBrowser in templates with @if to render different content on server and client. This causes hydration mismatches and layout shifts. Use afterNextRender instead.
Setting providers on the server

On the server side, providers configured with useValue keep their value across multiple requests until restart. If you want to generate a new value for each request, use a factory provider with useFactory.

Accessing Request and Response via DI

items: REQUEST: Provides access to the current request object (standard Web API Request) to inspect headers, cookies, and URL.
RESPONSE_INIT: Provides access to response initialization options (ResponseInit) to dynamically set status codes and headers at runtime.
REQUEST_CONTEXT: Provides access to additional context passed to handle().

Caching data when using HttpClient

HttpClient caches outgoing network requests when running on the server. This data is serialized and transferred to the browser as part of the initial HTML to prevent duplicate HTTP requests during initial application rendering.

blocks.text: Security

For SSR applications, safeguard against Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) by restricting allowed backend hosts and preventing client authentication tokens from being forwarded to untrusted third-party services.
